title: The body: its parts
hook: like a bag of mixed grain opened and looked at: hair, nails, teeth, skin (MN 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sampajanna, clear knowing, and your line was even this. Which chore did you do knowingly? Day two hundred fifty-three.

Think about how much of a day goes into what the body looks like. The mirror in the morning. The photo you retake four times. The comparison that slips in while scrolling. We tend to see the body as one thing, a whole picture, to be judged as good or bad. The Satipatthana Sutta does something different. It opens the body up, piece by piece, with the calm of a farmer checking stored grain. Today: the body, its parts.
screen: `THE MIRROR, THE RETAKEN PHOTO.` → `ONE PICTURE, JUDGED.` → `PIECE BY PIECE.`

segments.voice: The practitioner reviews this very body, the sutta says, from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin and, in the sutta's blunt word, full of many kinds of impurity. Then comes the list: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and on inward, organs and fluids, thirty-one parts in all in the sutta's list. Later tradition added the brain to make thirty-two. And then the image. It's like a bag with an opening at both ends, full of mixed grain: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, sesame, husked rice. A person with good eyes opens it and looks: this is rice, these are beans, this is sesame. Notice the tone. The person with the grain bag isn't disgusted, and isn't admiring. They're just sorting, clearly. That's the heart of the practice. In the Buddhist tradition, this contemplation is used to loosen two strong pulls: vanity about the body and craving for other bodies. Some teachers stress the unattractiveness of the parts; others, especially today, stress simple, neutral seeing. Either way, the point is not to hate the body. It's to see it as it is: not a single image to be judged, but a working collection of many things, all doing their jobs. Hair is hair. Teeth are teeth. The picture in the mirror loosens its grip a little.
screen: `FROM THE SOLES UP, THE HEAD DOWN.` · `HAIR, NAILS, TEETH, SKIN.` · `A BAG OF MIXED GRAIN, OPENED.` · `SORTING, NOT JUDGING.` · then, large: `A BAG OF GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Name ten parts of your body, slowly, feeling each one if you can, with the calm of someone sorting grain. Hair. Nails. Teeth. Skin. Bones. Muscles. Heart. Lungs. Blood. Breath. No judging any of them, no admiring or wincing. Just this is that. If any part is painful or hard to think about today, skip it gently and move on. The bell holds the time.
The body, its parts. Opened like a bag of mixed grain and sorted calmly: hair, nails, teeth, skin, each one just what it is.
Your line: a bag of grain. Today, when the mirror starts judging, try sorting instead: skin, hair, eyes, each one just doing its job. Day two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, the first five parts (hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin) are traditionally taught to new monks and nuns at ordination; the contemplation of the thirty-two parts is recited and practiced to loosen vanity and craving.

match.prompt: match each piece of the simile.
pairs: hill rice, red rice, beans, sesame
the count once the brain is added

myth: the practice is meant to make you hate your body
it's for seeing clearly and loosening vanity and craving, not for self-hatred.
the sutta's list has thirty-one parts; later tradition added the brain
the familiar count of thirty-two comes from the later list.
the grain simile is about sorting calmly
the person just sees: this is rice, these are beans.

fork.setup: you open a bag of mixed grain. what does the person in the sutta do?
options: look and sort: this is rice, these are beans.
admire how beautiful the grain is.
fork.reveal: the person with good eyes simply sees each thing for what it is. the body is looked at the same way.

trapdoor: what you thought: this practice is about finding the body gross.
what it means: seeing the body clearly as many parts, not one image to judge.
what a scholar hears: MN 10 lists thirty-one parts; the Khuddakapāṭha and later texts add the brain (matthaluṅga) to make thirty-two, and the first five are taught at ordination.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the parts of the body

notes: Sensitivity: this contemplation (asubha / paṭikūlamanasikāra) can be hard for people with eating disorders or body image struggles; the script frames it as neutral sorting and invites skipping any part. Please confirm the framing is faithful and acceptable.
Thirty-one parts in MN 10, thirty-two with the brain in the Khuddakapāṭha: confirm.
The grains in the simile (hill paddy, paddy, green gram, cow-peas, sesame, husked rice) vary by translation; the script simplifies them. Please check.
Ordination teaching of the first five parts (tacapañcaka): confirm.
Audit 2026-09-30: the paraphrase 'full of many kinds of things' hid the sutta's own word (asuci, impure); it now says so plainly, with the neutral-sorting framing kept.
